T1A01: Part 97.1 lists five purposes of the Amateur Radio Service, and one of them is advancing skills in the technical and communication phases of the radio art. Ham radio is not a personal communications service for the general public (that is closer to CB or FRS), and contesting is an activity hams enjoy, not a stated purpose. Since A and B are wrong, 'All these choices' is wrong too.
T1A02: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) writes and enforces the rules for amateur radio in the US; they are found in Title 47 CFR Part 97. The ARRL is a private membership organization that advocates for hams but has no regulatory authority. Homeland Security does not regulate amateur radio.
T1A03: 97.119(b)(2) says use of a standard phonetic alphabet as an aid for correct station identification is 'encouraged' when using phone. It is never mandatory. Memory tip: phonetics (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie...) help the other station copy your call sign correctly, so the FCC encourages them but does not require them.
T1A04: The FCC no longer mails paper licenses. After your exam results are processed, the FCC sends an email (to the address you provided, which is required under 97.23) containing a link to download your official license grant. The volunteer examiners do not issue the license.
T1A05: Your license exists once it appears in the FCC's Universal Licensing System (ULS) database. The CSCE from your exam session only proves you passed the exam elements, and the NCVEC does not grant licenses. The ULS database is the official record.
T1A06: 97.203(d) limits automatically controlled beacons on HF to specific segments, and the only one available in Technician HF territory is 28.200-28.300 MHz on 10 meters. That is where you can listen for 10-meter propagation beacons to see if the band is open.
T1A07: Part 97.3(a)(41) defines a space station as an amateur station located more than 50 km above the Earth's surface. It has nothing to do with whether it is crewed or whether it is a satellite. The ISS's amateur station qualifies because of its altitude. Key number: 50 km.
T1A08: Repeater pairs are recommended by a Volunteer Frequency Coordinator, a body set up and recognized by the local amateurs who run repeater and auxiliary stations (97.3(a)(22)). The FCC does not assign repeater channels and neither does the ITU. Coordination is a self-governing, volunteer system.
T1A09: Per 97.3(a)(22), the frequency coordinator is an entity recognized by amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations. In other words, the repeater community itself chooses its coordinator. The FCC does not appoint one.
T1A10: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) operates under civil defense authority. 97.407(a) requires that a RACES station's control operator hold an amateur license AND be certified as enrolled in a civil defense organization. ARES membership or an ARRL recommendation is not what the rule requires.
T1A11: 97.101(d) states that no amateur operator shall willfully or maliciously interfere with or cause interference to any radio communication or signal. International contacts on VHF/UHF and third-party traffic on digital modes are both legal (within the rules), so only B is prohibited.
T1B01: Technicians have 10-meter phone (voice) privileges from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz (97.301(e)). The other ranges are partly CW/data segments or outside Tech phone privileges. Memory tip: 'Tech voice on 10 is 28.3 to 28.5.'
T1B02: Any Technician or higher licensee may contact the ISS on its VHF/UHF amateur frequencies, because Techs have full privileges on 2 meters and 70 cm. No NASA approval is required to make a contact (scheduled school contacts are a separate ARISS program).
T1B03: The 6-meter band runs from 50 to 54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz (the national 6-meter FM simplex calling frequency) is inside it. 49.00 MHz is just below the band, 28.50 MHz is 10 meters, and 222.15 MHz is 1.25 meters.
T1B04: 146.52 MHz is the national 2-meter FM simplex calling frequency. The 2-meter band is 144-148 MHz. Wavelength check: 300 / 146 MHz is about 2 meters.
T1B05: Technicians may use data/digital modes such as FT8 on part of 10 meters (28.000-28.300 MHz) and on all of their VHF/UHF bands, including 6 meters and 2 meters. So every listed band qualifies.
T1B06: On HF, Technician voice privileges exist only on 10 meters (28.300-28.500 MHz). Techs also have CW on parts of 80, 40, and 15 meters, but no phone there. The 30-meter band is CW/data only for General and above.
T1B07: The bottom 100 kHz of 6 meters (50.0-50.1 MHz) and 2 meters (144.0-144.1 MHz) are restricted to CW only by 97.305. These segments are used for weak-signal CW work and beacons.
T1B08: In bands where amateurs are a secondary user, the primary users (such as government radar) have priority. Amateurs may share the band but must not cause harmful interference to primary-service stations and must accept interference from them (97.303).
T1B09: Your displayed frequency may be slightly off (calibration error), the transmitter may drift, and your signal occupies bandwidth on either side of the carrier (sidebands). Any of these could put part of your signal outside the band, which is a violation. That is why every reason listed is correct.
T1B10: On the amateur bands above 50 MHz, SSB phone is permitted in at least some segment of each band, not just the General-class portions, and not only on repeaters. Technicians commonly use SSB around 50.125 and 144.200 MHz for weak-signal contacts.
T1B11: Technicians operating in their HF segments (80, 40, 15 and 10 meters) are limited to 200 watts PEP output (97.313). This is less than the 1500 watt maximum allowed for General and higher on most HF bands.
T1B12: Above 30 MHz (VHF and up), Technicians enjoy full privileges, which includes the general amateur limit of 1500 watts PEP output (97.313(b)), with some specific exceptions (for example, near certain government installations). Of course you should always use the minimum power necessary (97.313(a)).
T1C01: The FCC currently issues new licenses only in three classes: Technician, General, and Amateur Extra. Novice, Technician Plus, and Advanced licenses can still be renewed by existing holders but are no longer issued to new licensees.
T1C02: Any licensed amateur may apply for a vanity call sign (97.19). However, the call signs you are eligible for depend on your license class. For example, short 1x2 calls are reserved for Extras.
T1C03: 97.117 allows international communications that are incidental to the purposes of the amateur service plus remarks of a personal character. Business communications are prohibited for all amateur communications, including international ones.
T1C04: 97.23 requires every licensee to keep a current email address on file with the FCC. Failure to provide one, or being unreachable at the address on file, can result in revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license.
T1C05: Group D call signs are the 2x3 format starting with K or W: two prefix letters, a number, and three suffix letters (such as KF1XXX). These are what new Technicians and Generals are sequentially issued. 'KA1X' (2x1) and 'W1XX' (1x2) are Group A formats reserved for Amateur Extras.
T1C06: 97.5 and 97.11 permit you to operate from a US-documented vessel (or craft) in international waters, with the permission of the master (captain). The FCC rules travel with a US-registered vessel, so your US license is valid there.
T1C07: You may apply to renew your license within 90 days before its expiration date. Applying earlier than that is not accepted.
T1C08: Amateur licenses are issued for a ten-year term (97.25). Renewal is free at the FCC (the $35 application fee does not apply to renewals).
T1C09: If your license expires, you have a two-year grace period to renew it without retesting (97.21). After two years the license is gone and you must pass the exams again.
T1C10: You may transmit once your license grant appears in the FCC's ULS database. Passing the exam (the CSCE) alone does not give a brand-new licensee transmitting privileges. The ARRL website is not an official record, and the FCC no longer mails licenses.
T1C11: During the two-year grace period you may renew, but you may NOT transmit. An expired license gives no operating privileges until the renewal is granted.
T1D01: 97.111(a)(1) prohibits communications with any country whose administration has notified the ITU (International Telecommunication Union) that it objects to such communications. The ARRL and IARU are private organizations without power to ban contacts.
T1D02: Broadcasting, meaning transmissions intended for the general public, is prohibited in the amateur service. One-way transmissions are allowed for specific purposes, such as code practice, information bulletins of interest to amateurs, and telecommand/telemetry.
T1D03: Messages encoded to obscure their meaning are generally prohibited. The exception is control commands sent to space stations or model craft (97.211(b), 97.215(b)), where encryption prevents unauthorized persons from commandeering the craft.
T1D04: Music is prohibited on the amateur bands except when incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications (for example, retransmitting NASA audio that happens to include music).
T1D05: You may announce amateur radio equipment for sale or trade as long as it is your own (or a close relative's) equipment and you are not doing it on a regular basis, meaning you are not running a business over the air.
T1D06: 97.113(a)(4) prohibits obscene or indecent language on the amateur bands. There is no official list of banned words. Any such language is prohibited.
T1D07: An auxiliary station transmits point-to-point communications within a system of amateur stations. A link that carries audio from a repeater's remote receiver to its main transmitter is a classic example.
T1D08: Amateurs generally cannot be paid to operate. One exception (97.113(a)(3)(iii)) is a teacher who operates as part of classroom instruction at an educational institution, where the teacher may be paid as part of their job.
T1D09: Amateur stations may help with news gathering or broadcasting only when the communications directly relate to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, and no other means is available. This typically comes up during disasters.
T1D10: Part 97 defines broadcasting as transmissions intended for reception by the general public. Amateur stations communicate with other amateurs, not with the public at large, so broadcasting is prohibited.
T1D11: Transmissions used to control model craft (RC planes, boats, cars) don't need station identification (97.215), provided the transmitter is labeled with the licensee's call sign and contact information. All other transmissions require ID, including brief tuning and low-power tests.
T1D12: Test transmissions are still amateur transmissions, so you must identify your station as usual (every 10 minutes and at the end). There are no special time windows and no FCC notification requirements.
T1E01: Every amateur station that transmits must have a control operator; there are no exceptions. Even a repeater under automatic control has a control operator who is responsible, even though that person is not at the controls at every moment.
T1E02: Satellite operation has no special license class or certification requirement. Anyone whose license permits transmitting on the satellite's uplink frequency may be the control operator. For most satellites, Technicians qualify because the uplinks are on 2 meters or 70 cm.
T1E03: The station licensee designates who the control operator will be (97.103(b)). When you operate your own station, you are normally both licensee and control operator.
T1E04: Transmitting privileges are set by the license class of the control operator, not the station owner. For example, if an Extra lets a Technician operate the Extra's station without supervision, only Technician privileges apply.
T1E05: The control point is the location where the control operator function is performed, meaning where the operator who controls the station sits. This could be miles away from the transmitter or antenna during remote operation.
T1E06: A Technician may never be the control operator on frequencies reserved for Extras, regardless of whose station it is. Privileges come from your own license class. (If an Extra is the control operator, the Tech could speak as a third party, but the Extra is then the one in control.)
T1E07: When someone else is the control operator, both the control operator and the station licensee are responsible for proper operation (97.103(a)). The owner cannot escape responsibility by handing the microphone to another ham.
T1E08: Automatic control means the station operates without the control operator being at the control point, as a repeater does. The rules allow certain stations, such as repeaters, to operate this way.
T1E09: Any amateur station may be remotely controlled (97.109(c)), as long as a control operator is at the control point and in control through a link. Remote control is different from automatic control.
T1E10: Part 97 remote control means the control operator is at a control point away from the station and controls it through a control link, such as operating your home station over the internet. Controlling model craft is 'telecommand', not remote control of a station.
T1E11: Per 97.3(a)(13), a control operator is the amateur operator designated by the station licensee to be responsible for the station's transmissions and for complying with the FCC rules.
T1F01: If an FCC representative asks, the station licensee must make the station and its records available for inspection at any time (97.103(c)). No warrant or advance notice is required. Keeping a license is conditional on agreeing to this.
T1F02: Tactical call signs are fine for convenience during events, but you must still give your FCC call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it. The tactical call does not replace your legal identification.
T1F03: 97.119(a) requires you to identify at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of the communication. You are not required to identify at the beginning (though it is good practice).
T1F04: When identifying by voice, you must use English (97.119(b)(2)). You may carry on the rest of the conversation in another language, but your call sign must be given in English.
T1F05: A station transmitting phone may identify by voice OR by CW (Morse code). Many repeaters identify in CW. Both are permitted methods.
T1F06: When adding a self-assigned indicator (such as a region number when operating away from home), the FCC allows words like 'stroke', 'slant', or 'slash' on phone. All these are acceptable.
T1F07: A non-licensed person may talk to a foreign station (third-party communications) only if the US has a third-party agreement with that foreign country (97.115(a)(2)). The unlicensed person does not need to be a US citizen.
T1F08: Third-party communications are messages from the control operator (first party) to another station's control operator (second party) on behalf of someone else (the third party). For example, letting a non-ham friend speak over your station or relaying a message for them.
T1F09: A repeater station receives on one frequency and simultaneously retransmits on another (97.3(a)(40)). This extends the range of low-power mobile and handheld radios.
T1F10: If a repeater automatically retransmits a rule violation, the control operator of the originating station is responsible (97.205(g)), not the repeater operator or owner.
T1F11: To get a club station license, the club must have at least four members (97.5(b)(2)). The trustee does not need to be an Extra, and ARRL registration is not required.
